content: Alternative institutional settings for childbirth have been developed to cater to pregnant women who prefer minimal or no medical intervention. These settings may provide care throughout pregnancy and delivery or only during labor. They can be integrated within hospitals or operate as independent facilities. Examples of specially designed labor rooms include bedroom-like environments, ambient rooms, and Snoezelen rooms. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of care in alternative institutional birth environments compared to conventional hospital settings. A secondary aim was to determine whether factors such as staffing, architectural design, organizational models, or geographical location influenced the outcomes of these birth settings. The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched up to March 30, 2012, to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria encompassed all randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing alternative institutional birth settings to conventional ones. Standard Cochrane methods were employed for data collection and analysis, with two reviewers independently assessing the methodological quality of the studies. Data extraction was performed in duplicate, and results were presented as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of ten trials involving 11,795 women met the inclusion criteria. No trials specifically examined freestanding birth centers or Snoezelen rooms. Allocation to an alternative birth setting was associated with several positive outcomes. Women in these settings were more likely to experience labor and delivery without intrapartum analgesia or anesthesia (six trials, n = 8,953; RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.33), achieve spontaneous vaginal birth (eight trials, n = 11,202; RR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.05), breastfeed at six to eight weeks postpartum (one trial, n = 1,147; RR 1.04, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.06), and report very positive views of their care (two trials, n = 1,207; RR 1.96, 95% CI 1.78 to 2.15). Conversely, allocation to an alternative setting was associated with a reduced likelihood of epidural analgesia (eight trials, n = 10,931; RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.87), oxytocin augmentation of labor (eight trials, n = 11,131; RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.88), instrumental vaginal birth (eight trials, n = 11,202; RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.99), and episiotomy (eight trials, n = 11,055; RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.90). There was no significant effect on other adverse maternal or neonatal outcomes. The presence of the same or separate staff in these settings did not appear to influence outcomes. However, it was not possible to draw definitive conclusions regarding the effects of caregiver continuity or specific architectural features of the birth environment. In several trials, the design characteristics of the alternative settings were confounded by differences in organizational care models, such as the use of separate staff or greater continuity of caregiver, making it challenging to isolate the independent effects of the physical environment. In conclusion, hospital-based birth centers are associated with lower rates of medical interventions during labor and delivery, as well as higher levels of maternal satisfaction, without increasing risks to mothers or newborns.
